papers.title_in_file: Variational Denoising for Variational Quantum Eigensolver
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, QAE and denoising method, results (all experiments), conclusion. Supplemental material [26] is not in the file and was not read.
papers.what_it_is: A Fujitsu letter proposing a quantum autoencoder trained on noisy VQE output states to improve energy estimates and ground-state fidelity, tested in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report that their variational denoising method decreases energy estimation errors and increases fidelities with ground states compared with the noisy input data, for the H2, LiH and BeH2 molecular Hamiltonians and the transverse field Ising model, even when only noisy data is used for training.
quotes: Our approach can significantly decrease energy estimation errors and increase fidelities with ground states compared to noisy input data for the H2, LiH, and BeH2 molecular Hamiltonians, and the transverse field Ising model.
even when using noisy data for training, the average performance of our method improves the ground state energy estimation with small fluctuation
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The text body shows no BeH2 experiment; that molecule appears only in the abstract (its results are likely in the supplement).

assertions.value: The authors state that for the one-dimensional transverse field Ising model their method can reduce the energy error by nearly an order of magnitude, while increasing the number of spins can make the problem harder.
quotes: While increasing N can make the problem harder
our method can reduce the error by nearly an order of magnitude
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QAE circuit is run in a well-controlled platform without the effect of quantum noise, and that the noisy data is produced by a noisy quantum channel applied to the VQE circuits or by early stopping of the optimizer.
quotes: we consider the QAE circuit in a well-controlled platform without the effect of quantum noise
The noisy data can be considered as the state generated from a noisy quantum channel applied to the VQE circuits
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Results, p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported gains are for simulated denoising of the QAE itself; no hardware run of the denoiser is reported in the main text.

assertions.value: The authors report that when the QAE is trained on high noise-level data, where the VQE output states have a low overlap with the ground state, irrelevant information leaks out at the bottleneck and the decoder cannot reconstruct the ground state.
quotes: However, if we train the QAE with high noise-level data where the VQE output states have a low overlap with the ground state, irrelevant information leaks out at the bottleneck, preventing the decoder from sequentially reconstructing the ground state (blue lines).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation observation from one study.

papers.title_in_file: Depth optimization of CNOT ladder circuits
papers.version_note: The file name says Depth-Optimization-of-Ansatz-Circuits-for-Variational-Quantum; the file title is Depth optimization of CNOT ladder circuits (arXiv 2511.13256v2). Same paper, retitled.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Sections II to V and Appendix A (pp.1-6). Reference list not read.
papers.what_it_is: A paper replacing each CNOT in a CNOT ladder with a measurement-based equivalent to get constant CNOT depth, with an error analysis of when that helps.

assertions.value: The authors state that in their non-unitary construction the CNOT depth stays constant and equal to 2 regardless of the register qubit count, and that circuit width, CNOT count and measurement count are smaller than in the two other methods that reach the same depth.
assertions.anchor: Section II and Table I, p.2
quotes: We see that the CNOT depth can be kept constant and equal to 2 regardless of the register qubit count.
but in our case circuit width, CNOT count, and measurement count are smaller than existing approaches
assertions.certainty_reason: Circuit-characteristics count in Table I, p.2; Appendix A proves the measurement-based CNOT equivalence, p.5.
assertions.reader_inference: The depth and width counts are for the paper's construction on an ideal device; they are not hardware runs.

assertions.value: The authors state that, under their error analysis, the choice between the unitary and the constant-depth construction depends on the relative difference between CNOT and idling error rates, and that the method is most effective where CNOT error probabilities are low compared with qubit idling error probabilities.
assertions.anchor: Abstract, Section IV and Section V, pp.1-5
quotes: Our error analysis shows that the choice between these two constructions depends on the relative difference between CNOT and idling error rates.
is most effective for platforms where CNOT error probabilities are relatively low compared to qubit idling error probabilities
assertions.certainty_reason: Result of a model-based fidelity-bound analysis, not a proof or a hardware run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the error analysis uses a twirling approximation that removes non-Pauli noise, that real quantum computers are also expected to show non-Pauli noise, and that fidelity is compared through a lower bound because exact simulation of large circuits is practically impossible.
quotes: even though in real quantum computers non-Pauli noise is also expected to be present
it is practically impossible to simulate the effect of quantum noise on classical computers and calculate the exact value of fidelity
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of its noise-model limits, Section IV, p.4.

papers.title_in_file: Benchmarking Adaptative Variational Quantum Algorithms on QUBO Instances
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, algorithms, experimental protocol, results text, conclusions, appendix. Result tables II to IV were seen only as garbled text and were not used for numbers.
papers.what_it_is: A noise-free simulation benchmark of three adaptative variational algorithms (EVQE, VAns, RA-VQE) and fixed-structure QAOA on three QUBO problem types.

assertions.value: The authors report that the adaptative algorithms do not provide an advantage in approximation ratio, because the value obtained with all methods is always close to 1.
assertions.anchor: Section IV-A and Section V, pp.3-5
quotes: Our results show that the adaptative algorithms do not provide an advantage in terms of approximation ratio, since the value obtained with all methods is always close to 1.
all the algorithms achieve highly accurate solutions with approximation ratios close to 1
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors report that the adaptative algorithms need a low number of gates, in particular cnot gates, while QAOA needs a larger number of both; VAns builds circuits with the lowest number of gates and almost always a depth of 1.
quotes: The adaptative algorithms require a low number of gates, in particular cnot gates, while QAOA requires a larger number of both.
VAns builds circuits with the lowest number of gates and cnot gates
VAns excels in producing shallow circuits, almost always with a depth of 1
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one benchmark.

assertions.value: The authors report, in additional experiments not shown in the paper, that limiting the QAOA parameter optimizer to 50 iterations gives approximation ratios averaging 0.96 for N=4, 0.81 for N=8, 0.78 for N=12 and 0.79 for N=15.
quotes: limiting the parameter optimizer to 50 iterations results in significantly lower approximation ratios, averaging at 0.96 for N=4, 0.81 for N=8, 0.78 for N=12, and 0.79 for N=15 across the different instances
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result the authors say is not included in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors do not show these experiments, so the figures cannot be checked from the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study covers MaxCut, Minimum Vertex Cover and Number Partitioning QUBO instances with N=4, 8, 12 and 15 variables, in noise-free scenarios, and that larger instances, noisy scenarios and real quantum hardware are left for future work.
quotes: we consider instances of different size, with N=4, 8, 12, and 15 variables
for solving QUBO problems in noise-free scenarios
the investigation of the performance of adaptative algorithms on larger problem instances and in noisy scenarios, as well as the evaluation of their effectiveness on real quantum hardware
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of scope, Section III-A and Section V.

papers.title_in_file: Toward Practical Quantum Machine Learning: A Novel Hybrid Quantum LSTM for Fraud Detection
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, literature review, preprocessing, methodology start, training, benchmarking, results, conclusion. Model-architecture equations skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid classical LSTM plus variational quantum circuit classifier for credit card fraud detection, simulated on a CPU and compared with a classical LSTM.

assertions.value: The authors report a training accuracy of 99.69% and a test accuracy of 95.33% for the hybrid model; on 1,500 test samples (750 fraud and 750 non-fraud) it misclassifies 45 non-fraud as fraud and 25 fraud as non-fraud.
assertions.anchor: Section VII-A and Section VIII, pp.6-8
quotes: the quantum hybrid model achieves a very high training accuracy of 99.69% and a test accuracy of 95.33%
out of the total 1,500 test samples (750 fraud and 750 non-fraud), the model misclassifies only a small fraction (45 non-fraud labeled as fraud and 25 fraud labeled as non-fraud)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one run on one synthetic dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The test set is a resampled, class-balanced subset, so the figures do not describe performance at a real fraud base rate.

assertions.value: The authors state that their hybrid approach outperforms the classical LSTM in key predictive metrics, particularly recall and F1 score, while the classical LSTM trains in under 2 seconds per epoch, significantly faster than the hybrid model.
assertions.anchor: Section VII-B and Section VIII, pp.8-9 (Table II)
quotes: our hybrid approach outperforms it in key predictive metrics, particularly in recall and F1 score
On average, the classical LSTM required under 2 seconds per epoch to train, which is significantly faster than the hybrid quantum model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical comparison from one study; the paper reports no repeated runs or significance test in the text read.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's per-epoch time for the hybrid is a classical-simulator time, so it does not show a quantum speed advantage; the accuracy gap over the baseline is small and from a single reported run.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dataset is synthetically generated, that a balanced subset of 10,000 transactions (5,000 fraudulent and 5,000 non-fraudulent) was used because of computational constraints, that the model runs on a CPU simulator without GPU acceleration, and that validation on actual quantum hardware is future work.
assertions.anchor: Sections II-C, IV-A and VIII, pp.2-9
quotes: The dataset used in this study is a synthetically generated credit card fraud dataset designed to mimic real-world transaction data.
Due to computational constraints, we select a balanced subset of 10,000 transactions, consisting of 5,000 fraudulent and 5,000 non-fraudulent transactions.
default.qubit simulator, which runs on the CPU without GPU acceleration
on validating the model on actual quantum hardware
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of dataset and platform scope, Sections IV-A and VIII.

assertions.value: The authors state that training accuracy is significantly higher than validation and test accuracy and that this suggests the hybrid model may be overfitting to the training data.
quotes: This discrepancy suggests that the model may be overfitting to the training data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limitation, Section VII-A item 5.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Computing and Cybersecurity Education: A Novel Curriculum for Enhancing Graduate STEM Learning
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, curriculum design, evaluation sections 3.1 to 3.3 (partly), future adoption, conclusion. Student quotations list and figures skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A Penn State graduate hardware-security course with quantum security labs on IBM hardware, evaluated by pre- and post-surveys of a small cohort.

assertions.value: The authors report positive post-course survey means on a 4-point agreement scale, including value of the course (M=3.5), organization (M=3.67) and desire for careers in quantum computing and cybersecurity (M=3.67).
quotes: Overall, students found the course valuable (M=3.5) and well-organized (M=3.67).
Most students expressed a desire for future careers involving quantum computing and cybersecurity (M=3.67)
on a scale from 1 to 4 (1 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree)
assertions.certainty_reason: Self-reported survey results from one small cohort.
assertions.reader_inference: These are satisfaction and interest ratings, not measured skill gains.

assertions.value: The authors state that the small sample size (N=7) limits the generalizability of findings, and that a planned focus group could not be conducted because of insufficient voluntary participation.
quotes: The small sample size (N=7) in the current study limits the generalizability of findings, so future offerings will aim for a larger cohort.
a focus group could not be conducted as planned due to insufficient voluntary participation
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limit, Section 4, p.13.
assertions.reader_inference: Only five of the seven students completed the pre-survey, so pre/post comparisons rest on even fewer respondents.

assertions.value: The authors claim that, to the best of their knowledge, this is the first comprehensive attempt to advance quantum cybersecurity education through a hands-on, activity-based approach that integrates both classical and quantum concepts.
quotes: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive attempt to advance quantum cybersecurity education through a hands-on, activity-based approach that integrates both classical and quantum concepts.
assertions.certainty_reason: Priority claim by the authors with no systematic search shown.

papers.title_in_file: On the Transfer of Knowledge in Quantum Algorithms
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Section II fundamentals, Section III use cases UC1 to UC3 (text, not the Table IV cell values), Section III-B, Section V. Section IV challenges only skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A framework and taxonomy paper for transfer of knowledge in quantum computing, with three small use cases on reverse annealing, multitasking QAOA and sequential VQE.

assertions.value: The authors state that their experiments confirmed that transfer of knowledge can enhance performance, improving solution quality and consistency in quantum annealing (UC1), increasing success rates in multitasking QAOA (UC2), and accelerating convergence in VQE through parameter reuse (UC3).
quotes: improving solution quality and consistency in quantum annealing (UC1), increasing success rates in multitasking QAOA (UC2), and accelerating convergence in VQE through parameter reuse (UC3)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical results from three small use cases in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The use cases are small (a 50-node MaxCut instance, the H2 molecule); the paper's text gives no significance tests.

assertions.value: The authors report that in reverse annealing seeded from related MaxCut_50_X instances, result quality improves significantly as problem similarity increases, and that seeding from the unrelated instance MaxCut_50_100 does worse than forward annealing (negative transfer).
assertions.anchor: Section III-A, UC1, p.6 (Fig. 3, Table IV)
quotes: the quality of the results improves significantly as the similarity of the problems increases
the results for the unrelated instance MaxCut_50_100 highlight the potentially harmful effects of a negative ToK, as the RA process performs even worse than the forward annealing approach
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one use case on one device.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results are constrained by current quantum hardware limitations, and that multitask transfer remains constrained by coherence challenges while sequential transfer proves more practical and effective.
assertions.anchor: Section III-B and Section V, pp.11-12
quotes: These results, while promising, are naturally constrained by the current limitations of quantum hardware.
although multitask transfer remains constrained by coherence challenges, sequential transfer proves to be a more practical and effective approach
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limits, Section III-B and Section V.
assertions.reader_inference: The statement that benefits will grow with larger problems and better hardware is an expectation, not a tested result.

papers.title_in_file: Large gradients via correlation in random parameterized quantum circuits
papers.version_note: File is arXiv 2005.12200v2 (authors Volkoff and Coles); same paper as the record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, background, Section 2.1 start, conclusions. Proofs in Sections 3 to 5 and appendices were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper proving that correlating parameters across circuit layers can avoid barren plateau landscapes in some random parameterized quantum circuits, including variational Grover search.

assertions.value: The authors prove that reducing the dimensionality of the parameter space by using circuit modules with spatially or temporally correlated gate layers can circumvent the vanishing gradient phenomenon.
quotes: we prove that reducing the dimensionality of the parameter space by utilizing circuit modules containing spatially or temporally correlated gate layers can allow one to circumvent the vanishing gradient phenomenon
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as proved in the Abstract, p.1; proofs in Sections 3 to 5 (not read).
assertions.reader_inference: The result holds for the specific circuit families analyzed, not for correlated circuits in general.

assertions.value: The authors state that their bounds on cost function variation imply a transition between vanishing gradients and efficient trainability in variational versions of Grover's algorithm, and that trainability requires a circuit depth that coincides, up to a logarithmic correction, with the optimal oracle complexity of quantum unstructured search.
quotes: our bounds on cost function variation imply a transition between vanishing gradients and efficient trainability
requires a circuit depth that coincides (up to a logarithmic correction) with the optimal oracle complexity of quantum unstructured search
assertions.certainty_reason: Main result, Section 5 as described in the Introduction, p.2.
assertions.reader_inference: Circuit depth at the optimal oracle complexity is exponential in the number of qubits, so this is trainability at exponential cost, not a general fix.

assertions.value: The authors state that a tradeoff is expected between algorithm complexity and trainability via parameter correlation, and that their global-cost QAOA example requires exponential depth to avoid the barren plateau with a correlated circuit.
quotes: a tradeoff is expected between algorithm complexity and trainability via parameter correlation
which requires exponential depth in order to avoid the BPL phenomenon for a correlated RPQC
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limit, Conclusions, p.14.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Federated Learning With Quantum Networks
papers.partial_detail: Whole paper body read (abstract through conclusion); references skipped.
papers.what_it_is: A short workshop paper simulating ring-topology quantum federated learning with variational quantum circuits and quantum weights on a toy classification dataset.

assertions.value: The authors claim in the conclusion that their study establishes the quantum advantage of their QFL model over classical FL models using the make-circles dataset.
quotes: Our study establishes the quantum advantage of our QFL model over classical FL models using the make-circles dataset.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' claim; the Discussion of the same paper says a significant advantage is hard to show on this dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: This claim conflicts with the paper's own Section 5.3.2, which reports similar performance for classical and quantum models; no numerical advantage is given in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical FL model and the QFL model with classical weights perform similarly, converging around round 25 and round 20 of training respectively, and state that the dataset is very simple so it is difficult to show a significant quantum advantage.
quotes: The dataset that we use in this work is very simple; because of this, it can be difficult to show a significnat quantum advantage.
the performance of the CFL model and QFL model with classical weights are similar, converging around round 25 and round 20 of training, respectively
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one toy dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that they perform binary classification of the make-circles dataset, a toy dataset, with 960 training data and 240 testing data, run for 100 rounds of training with 5 local epochs per client, in a ring topology.
quotes: We perform binary classification of the make-circles dataset, a toy dataset what is particularly useful for visualizing classification algorithms.
960 training data and 240 testing data.
We run the models each for 100 rounds of training, with 5 local epochs for each client.
assertions.certainty_reason: Paper's own statement of its experimental setup, Section 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that they only mimic the use of quantum teleportation in their quantum communication model, and that their techniques do not truly demonstrate teleportation of quantum weights.
quotes: We only mimic the use of quantum teleportation in our quantum communication model; our techniques, while feasible, do not truly demonstrate teleportation of quantum weights.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own stated limit, Section 5.3.1.
